To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

employers who offer a choice of plans have lower premiums, primarily because they enroll employees in less generous plans and cover a greater share of workers, and that the relationship between offering choice and premiums is consistent with employers offering choices to accommodate diverse employee preferences.

1) offering choice is associated with lower average premiums, 2) the lower average premiums are primarily driven by the fact that employees are enrolled in more cost-effective plans (i.e. plans with lower premiums and higher deductibles), and 3) employers offering choice cover a greater proportion (but not a greater number) of workers.
employers who offer health plan choice have lower average health insurance premiums and cover a larger proportion of employees than those who do.

the effect of offering health plan choice to workers on the cost and coverage of health benefits.
how employers use the health insurance market to provide benefits to their employees.

offering employees choice in their health plan is associated with a number of positive effects on the health care system.

the results of this study suggest that offering employees a choice of plans is not a strategy for employers to shift costs onto workers or to reduce the proportion of workers covered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between offering choice and insurance costs is not straightforward.
the availability of choice is associated with lower premiums and higher coverage rates.
offering choice to workers is not necessarily a bad idea.

the availability of choice is associated with lower premiums and greater coverage, and that these relationships are consistent with employers using choice to accommodate diverse employee preferences.
